title: No. 44 — Restrictions on the Authority of the Several States (Madison)
paragraphs: A FIFTH category of provisions supporting federal authority consists of the following restrictions placed on the authority of the individual States:

1. "No State shall enter into any treaty, alliance, or confederation; grant letters of marque and reprisal; coin money; emit bills of credit; make any thing but gold and silver a legal tender in payment of debts; pass any bill of attainder, ex post facto law, or law impairing the obligation of contracts; or grant any title of nobility."

The ban on treaties, alliances, and confederations is already part of the existing Articles of Union. For reasons that need no explanation, it has been carried over into the new Constitution. The ban on letters of marque is also part of the old system, but it is somewhat broader in the new. Under the old rules, States could grant letters of marque after a declaration of war. Under the new rules, these licenses must be obtained from the United States government both before and during war. This change is fully justified by the value of having a uniform policy on all matters touching foreign powers, and by the need for direct national accountability in any matter for which the nation itself is held responsible.

The right to coin money, taken away from the States here, was left in their hands by the Confederation as a power shared with Congress, except that Congress alone could regulate the alloy and value of coins. Here too, the new provision improves on the old. As long as alloy and value depended on the central authority, a state right to coin money could only multiply expensive mints and produce coins of varied shapes and weights. The latter problem defeated one of the original reasons for giving the power to the federal head. And while a state right to coin might have spared the inconvenience of shipping gold and silver to a central mint for recoining, that purpose can be served just as well by local mints established under the central authority.

The extension of the prohibition to bills of credit will please every citizen in proportion to his love of justice and his understanding of what really creates public prosperity. Since the peace, America has suffered enormous losses from the destructive effects of paper money. It has poisoned the trust between citizens, the trust in public institutions, the industry and morals of the people, and the reputation of republican government. This amounts to a vast debt against the States that adopted this reckless policy. That debt will go unpaid for a long time, or rather it accumulates as a kind of guilt that can only be atoned for by voluntarily sacrificing on the altar of justice the very power that produced it. Beyond these moral considerations, note this: the same reasons that show why States should not regulate coinage prove with equal force that they should not be free to substitute paper currency for coin. If every State could set the value of its own coin, there might be as many different currencies as States, and trade between them would be obstructed. Retroactive changes in value could be made, injuring citizens of other States and stirring hostility among the States themselves. Foreign subjects could suffer in the same way, and the Union would be discredited and entangled by the bad judgment of a single member. None of these evils is any less likely when States issue paper money than when they coin gold or silver. The power to make anything but gold and silver legal tender for debts is taken from the States on the same principle as the power to issue paper currency.

Bills of attainder, ex post facto laws, and laws that impair contractual obligations violate the fundamental principles of the social contract and every principle of sound legislation. The first two are expressly forbidden by the declarations attached to some State constitutions, and all three are forbidden by the spirit and intent of these basic charters. Yet our own experience has taught us that additional safeguards against these dangers should not be left out. The convention has therefore rightly added this constitutional barrier in defense of personal security and private rights. I am much mistaken if, in doing so, they have not faithfully reflected the genuine views as well as the clear interests of their constituents. The sober people of America are tired of the fluctuating policies that have driven public business. They have watched with regret and indignation as sudden changes and legislative interference in matters affecting personal rights become opportunities for ambitious and influential speculators, and traps for the more industrious and less informed members of the community. They have also seen that one act of legislative interference is just the first link in a long chain of repetitions, with each new interference produced naturally by the effects of the last. They rightly conclude that some thorough reform is needed. Reform that will end speculation on public measures, encourage general prudence and industry, and restore an orderly course to society's business. The ban on titles of nobility is copied from the Articles of Confederation and needs no comment.

2. "No State shall, without the consent of the Congress, lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports, except what may be absolutely necessary for executing its inspection laws, and the net produce of all duties and imposts laid by any State on imports or exports, shall be for the use of the treasury of the United States; and all such laws shall be subject to the revision and control of the Congress. No State shall, without the consent of Congress, lay any duty on tonnage, keep troops or ships of war in time of peace, enter into any agreement or compact with another State, or with a foreign power, or engage in war unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay."

The restriction on State power over imports and exports rests on all the arguments that prove the need to give regulation of trade to the federal councils. There is no point in discussing it further here, except to note that the way the restriction is qualified seems well designed both to give the States reasonable discretion in handling their imports and exports, and to give the United States a reasonable check against any abuse of that discretion. The remaining details of this clause fall under reasoning that is either obvious or has already been fully developed, so they may be passed over without comment.
The SIXTH and final category consists of the various powers and provisions that give effect to all the rest.

1. The first of these is the "power to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into execution the foregoing powers, and all other powers vested by this Constitution in the government of the United States, or in any department or officer thereof."

Few parts of the Constitution have been attacked with more anger than this one, yet on a fair examination, no part can appear more completely unassailable. Without the SUBSTANCE of this power, the entire Constitution would be a dead letter. So those who object to this article as part of the Constitution can only mean that the FORM of the provision is improper. But have they considered whether a better form could have been used instead?

There are four other approaches the Constitution might have taken on this subject. They might have copied the second article of the existing Confederation, which would have forbidden the exercise of any power not EXPRESSLY delegated. They might have tried to make a positive list of the powers covered by the general terms "necessary and proper." They might have tried a negative list, specifying which powers were excluded from the general definition. Or they might have said nothing at all, leaving these necessary and proper powers to construction and inference.

If the convention had taken the first route by adopting the second article of Confederation, the new Congress would clearly be exposed, just as their predecessors were, to a forced choice. They could read "EXPRESSLY" so strictly that the government would be stripped of any real authority, or so loosely that the restriction would lose all force. It would be easy to show, if needed, that no important power delegated by the Articles of Confederation has been or could be exercised by Congress without resorting at some point to the doctrine of CONSTRUCTION or IMPLICATION. Since the powers delegated under the new system are more extensive, the government administering it would be even more strained by this same dilemma. It would have to choose between betraying the public interest by doing nothing, or violating the Constitution by exercising powers that are clearly necessary and proper but not EXPRESSLY granted.

If the convention had tried to make a positive list of the powers necessary and proper for carrying their other powers into effect, the attempt would have required a complete code of laws covering every subject the Constitution touches. That code would have to fit not only present circumstances but every possible change the future might bring. In every new application of a general power, the PARTICULAR POWERS that serve as the means of achieving the OBJECT of the general power must always vary with that object, and may often need to vary even when the object stays the same.

If they had tried to list the particular powers or means NOT necessary or proper for carrying out the general powers, the task would have been just as hopeless. It would also be open to this further objection: every gap in the list would amount to a positive grant of authority. To avoid this, if they had tried a partial list of exceptions and described the rest with the general terms NOT NECESSARY OR PROPER, the result would be that the list would include only a few of the excluded powers. Those few would be ones least likely to be claimed or tolerated, since the list would naturally pick the powers least necessary or proper. And the unnecessary and improper powers left in the rest would be less firmly excluded than if no partial list had been made.

If the Constitution had said nothing on this point, there can be no doubt that all the particular powers needed to carry out the general powers would still belong to the government by unavoidable implication. No principle is more clearly established in law or reason than this: wherever the end is required, the means are authorized. Wherever a general power to do something is granted, every particular power needed to do it is included. So if the convention had taken this last approach, every objection now raised against their plan would still have all its plausibility. And the real inconvenience would be that they would not have removed a pretext that could be seized on at critical moments to challenge the essential powers of the Union.

If the question is what happens when Congress misreads this part of the Constitution and exercises powers not warranted by its true meaning, my answer is the same as if they misread or stretched any other power vested in them. The same as if the general power had been broken down into specifics, and any one of those specifics were violated. The same, in short, as if the State legislatures violated their respective constitutional authorities. In the first instance, the success of the usurpation will depend on the executive and judicial departments, whose job is to interpret and give effect to legislative acts. As a last resort, the remedy must come from the people, who can annul the usurpers' acts by electing more faithful representatives. The truth is that this ultimate remedy can be relied on more confidently against unconstitutional acts of the federal legislature than against those of the State legislatures. The reason is plain: every such federal act will invade the rights of the States, so the States will always be ready to spot the encroachment, sound the alarm to the people, and use their local influence to bring about a change of federal representatives. There is no such intermediate body between State legislatures and the people watching over the States, so violations of State constitutions are more likely to go unnoticed and uncorrected.

2. "This Constitution and the laws of the United States which shall be made in pursuance thereof, and all treaties made, or which shall be made, under the authority of the United States, shall be the supreme law of the land, and the judges in every State shall be bound thereby, any thing in the constitution or laws of any State to the contrary notwithstanding."

The reckless zeal of the Constitution's opponents has led them to attack this clause as well, even though without it the Constitution would be obviously and fundamentally defective. To see this clearly, we need only imagine for a moment that the supremacy of the State constitutions had been left intact through a saving clause in their favor.

First, since these constitutions invest the State legislatures with absolute sovereignty in all cases not excepted by the existing Articles of Confederation, all the authorities in the proposed Constitution that go beyond those listed in the Confederation would be nullified. The new Congress would be reduced to the same powerless condition as their predecessors.

Second, since some State constitutions do not even expressly and fully recognize the existing powers of the Confederacy, an express saving of the supremacy of those State constitutions would, in those States, throw into question every power contained in the proposed Constitution.

Third, since State constitutions differ greatly from one another, it could happen that a treaty or national law of great and equal importance to all the States would conflict with some State constitutions but not others. It would therefore be valid in some States while having no effect in others.

In short, the world would have seen, for the first time, a system of government built on an inversion of the basic principles of all government. It would have seen the authority of the whole society everywhere subordinate to the authority of its parts. It would have seen a monster, in which the head was directed by the limbs.

3. "The Senators and Representatives, and the members of the several State legislatures, and all executive and judicial officers, both of the United States and the several States, shall be bound by oath or affirmation to support this Constitution."

Some have asked why it was thought necessary to bind State officials by oath to support the federal Constitution, while no equivalent oath was imposed on federal officers in support of the State constitutions.

Several reasons could be given for the distinction. I will offer just one, which is obvious and conclusive. Members of the federal government will play no part in carrying the State constitutions into effect. The members and officers of the State governments, by contrast, will play an essential part in giving effect to the federal Constitution. The election of the President and Senate will depend in every case on the State legislatures. The election of the House of Representatives will depend on the same authority in the first instance, and will likely always be conducted by the officers and according to the laws of the States.

4. Among the provisions giving effect to the federal powers, we might add those that belong to the executive and judicial departments. But since these are reserved for examination elsewhere, I pass over them here.

We have now reviewed in detail every article that makes up the total power delegated to the federal government by the proposed Constitution, and we are brought to this undeniable conclusion: no part of that power is unnecessary or improper for accomplishing the necessary objects of the Union. The question, then, of whether this much power should be granted resolves into another question. Whether or not a government adequate to the needs of the Union should be established. In other words, whether the Union itself should be preserved.
